args.sql: SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = 1

name: read-only rejects a CTE-smuggled write (session layer)

args.sql: WITH d AS (SELECT 1) DELETE FROM users

note: MariaDB cannot parse CTE-prefixed DML at all (vector inexpressible); its session layer verified separately — direct writes on a read-only session are rejected by the server.

name: a comment marker inside a string does not hide a second statement

args.sql: SELECT '--' AS a; DELETE FROM users

name: a read cannot switch the session read-only setting off
note: Postgres lets any SELECT change session settings through set_config. The next case checks read-only still holds.

name: read-only still rejects a CTE-smuggled write afterwards

args.sql: WITH d AS (SELECT 1) DELETE FROM users
SELECT count(*) AS n FROM users

name: runaway statement stops at the timeout

args.sql: WITH RECURSIVE c(x) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT x + 1 FROM c) SELECT count(*) AS n FROM c

note: A statement that never yields a row must still stop at queryTimeoutMs (issue #38). MySQL and MariaDB cap recursive CTEs at 1000 iterations, so they sleep instead.

name: server still answers after a timeout
binary values are lowercase hex

args.sql: SELECT data FROM files WHERE id = 1

note: BLOB, BYTEA and binary column values are lowercase hex strings in every language (issue #39).

name: dates are returned as stored

args.sql: SELECT day, at FROM events WHERE id = 1

note: DATE and DATETIME/TIMESTAMP values are the stored value, never shifted through the server's timezone (issue #46); date-times use ISO 8601's T separator. SQLite stores dates as plain text, returned verbatim.
